name: Daily returns
brief:
A return is the change in price as a fraction of the price before it. Returns, not prices, are what every risk number is built from.

Write `daily_returns(prices)`. It takes closing prices in time order and returns a list with one return for each day after the first.
definition:
The simple return on day $t$ compares the close with the close the day before:

$$r_t = \dfrac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1$$

So $n$ prices give $n - 1$ returns. Return an empty list for fewer than two prices. Every price is positive.
constraints: $O(n)$ time, where $n$ is the number of prices.
Do not change the list you are given.
Standard library only. NumPy and pandas are not loaded.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Pair each price with the one before it. `zip(prices, prices[1:])` gives those pairs, yesterday first.
starter:
def daily_returns(prices):
    """Return the simple daily returns of prices,
    one fewer than there are prices."""
    # Your code here
    return []

tests.name: Empty list
tests.why: With no prices there are no returns. Return an empty list.

tests.name: Single price
tests.why: One price has nothing before it, so there are no returns yet.

tests.name: Two prices
tests.why: Two prices give one return: $\tfrac{105}{100} - 1 = 0.05$, a fraction, not 5.

tests.name: Flat prices
tests.why: A price that does not move has a return of exactly 0.

tests.name: Falling prices
tests.why: Divide by the day before, not by the first price. 150 to 120 is a fall of $\tfrac{30}{150} = 0.2$.

tests.name: Up then down
tests.why: A rise of 1.0 then a fall of 0.5 brings the price back. Returns are not symmetric.

tests.name: Whole-number prices
tests.why: With integer prices, `4 / 3` is still a float in Python 3. Make sure nothing rounds it.

tests.name: Daily closes
tests.why: Return every day after the first, in order, without rounding.

tests.name: Input left alone
tests.note: Calls your function, then returns the list it was given
tests.why: Your function changed the list it was given. Build a new list instead of popping or overwriting prices.

tests.name: Long series
tests.note: 100,000 prices from a seeded random walk; the last three returns are checked
tests.why: This test has 100,000 prices. Check that you return one value per day after the first, in order.

how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests, from an empty list to 100,000 prices. Lists are compared element by element, and each float counts when it is within a relative 1e-9 of the expected value.
where: Part of the 1.1 exit project: returns, annualised volatility and maximum drawdown from a CSV of daily prices.
solution:
def daily_returns(prices):
    # Each pair is (yesterday, today)
    return [today / yesterday - 1
            for yesterday, today in zip(prices, prices[1:])]
notes: `zip(prices, prices[1:])` pairs every price with the one after it and stops at the shorter list, so the last price has no partner.
Dividing by `yesterday` measures each move against the price it started from.
A list comprehension builds a new list, so the input is never changed.
prelude:
def _walk(n, seed, start, step):
    # Seeded random walk from an integer LCG, so every Python makes the same prices
    x = seed
    p = start
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648
        p = p * (1 + step * ((x % 2001 - 1000) / 1000))
        out.append(p)
    return out
